articles.title: Canada announces targets for new international student arrivals through 2029
articles.summary: The Canadian government has announced temporary immigration targets for 2027, 2028, and 2029 as part of the 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan, released on 5 November alongside the federal budget. The plan sets an annual cap of 370,000 study permits for new international student arrivals during those years.
articles.insight:
Canada’s 370,000-per-year cap on new study permits signals a deliberate move to stabilize international student numbers after recent growth and scrutiny, potentially shifting demand toward alternative destinations—but actual enrolment shifts depend on how strictly the cap is enforced and whether it affects perceived quality or post-study work prospects.  
Admissions teams should track Canadian visa processing times, provincial policy adjustments, and real-time source-market sentiment—especially among high-potential applicants from India, Nigeria, and China—to assess whether this cap meaningfully alters competitor attractiveness or creates near-term recruitment opportunities.

articles.title: Federal court scraps Trump’s four-year limit on international students’ stays
articles.summary: A federal court in Massachusetts has struck down a Department of Homeland Security rule that imposed a four-year limit on the stays of international students, exchange visitors, and foreign media representatives. The ruling reinstates the previous Duration of Status policy, which allowed these individuals to remain in the U.S. for the duration of their approved programs plus applicable grace periods.
articles.insight:
This ruling temporarily eases U.S. visa uncertainty for international students by restoring indefinite program-based stays, potentially improving the U.S.’s competitiveness against the UK, Australia, and New Zealand—though broader immigration sentiment and enforcement practices remain key demand drivers.  
Admissions teams should track how U.S. universities communicate this change to prospective students, monitor application trends from high-intent markets like India and China, and assess whether peer institutions adjust messaging or recruitment timelines in response.

articles.title: US proposes tougher Green Card sponsorship rules; what Indian graduates seeking EB-2 and EB-3 visas should know
articles.summary: The US Department of Labor has proposed stricter Green Card sponsorship rules under the PERM program, including longer job advertisements, stricter recruitment requirements, additional restrictions on employers that have conducted layoffs, and the removal of Schedule A exemptions. Published on November 17, 2026, the proposal is open for public comment and does not impact F-1, OPT, or STEM OPT eligibility.
articles.insight:
This proposal signals potential long-term tightening of US permanent residency pathways for Indian graduates, which may subtly influence perceptions of post-study settlement viability—though immediate impacts on student enrollment decisions remain uncertain given the proposal’s consultative stage and separation from temporary visa categories.  
Admissions teams should monitor public comment outcomes and final rule implementation timelines, while reviewing messaging around US career pathways to ensure transparency about evolving green card prospects without amplifying unwarranted concern among prospective Indian applicants.

articles.title: “Students are talking”: NUS president warns moving goalposts are costing Brand UK
articles.summary: Favour Samuel, the first international student to serve as president of NUS England, has warned that shifting immigration rules and visa refusals are damaging the UK’s global reputation among international students. She highlighted that students are openly sharing their negative experiences, which is eroding “Brand UK.”
articles.insight:
This news signals potential softening in UK appeal for international students, as visible policy volatility and negative peer narratives may dampen demand—though empirical enrolment data and regional variations mean the impact remains uncertain and likely uneven across source markets.  
Admissions teams should track real-time sentiment shifts in key feeder countries via social listening and agent feedback, while reviewing how their visa support, post-study work messaging, and comparative value propositions differentiate them amid growing global competition for mobile talent.
